openingMessage: Set your house in perfect order before you criticize the world.
openingWhy: Before we critique the operator's plan at the pre-job, the honest question: is our own trailer inspected, our bottles full, our forms real? On location, the crew whose house is in order is the crew that gets listened to when it counts.
leadershipThought: Nobody protects a location alone. The willingness to carry extra weight, communicate early, and check on the person next to you — that is coaching in action.

specialFocus.title: October 1 — New-Month Trailer Changeover
specialFocus.why: It's the first of the month, and the first of the month means every trailer gets reset TODAY — not by Friday, not 'when I'm back out there.' Fresh inspection paperwork, current workpacks, mask bags gone through, SCBA inspections documented. This paperwork is what the company man, an auditor, or an incident investigator pulls first — and a trailer still showing September paperwork on October 5th says we check boxes instead of equipment. The inspection only protects you if it actually happened, so put your hands on the gear, then sign the sheet.
specialFocus.standardLabel: Month-Start Changeover — Every Trailer, Day One
standard: September inspection sheets come DOWN and come IN — completed, signed, and turned in with the trailer paperwork. Last month's records get filed, never tossed and never left riding in the trailer.

Post the fresh October trailer inspection sheet and do the first inspection today — walk the trailer and put your hands on the equipment before you sign. A signature on an untouched trailer is worse than a blank sheet.
Swap in the new workpacks — current month, current revision, every trailer. Pull the old packs out so nobody grabs stale paperwork on location.
Open every mask bag — don't just count bags. Check the facepiece, seal, straps, and lens, confirm sizes, and re-tag each bag with the October inspection.

SCBA paperwork current on every pack: October inspection documented, bottle pressures checked, hydro dates verified. A pack with out-of-date paperwork comes out of service until it's inspected — no exceptions.
Find something wrong during the changeover — a bad strap, a scratched lens, a low bottle — that's a WIN. Tag it out, swap it, and write it up. That's exactly what this day is for.

scenarios.title: The Trailer That 'Looked Fine'
scenarios.body: A trailer sat on a long-running location all of September. The sheets got signed every month — from the truck. On October 1 a tech actually opens the mask bags and finds a facepiece with a cracked strap keeper that's been riding there for who knows how long. Nobody got hurt, but play it forward: an H2S hit, a tech grabs that mask under pressure, and the strap lets go. The changeover isn't paperwork — it's the one day a month we guarantee somebody physically touched every piece of emergency equipment we'd bet a life on.

scenarios.title: The Audit Pull
scenarios.body: A customer safety rep walks a location mid-October and asks for the trailer book. If the October inspection is there, signed on the 1st, with mask bags tagged and SCBA logs current — the conversation is over in two minutes and we look like exactly who we say we are. If September's sheet is still on the clipboard, every other thing we do right on that location is now in question. Day-one paperwork is the cheapest credibility we ever buy.

questions: Which trailers are you personally responsible for flipping today, and when will each one be done?
When you open a mask bag, what are the five things your hands and eyes actually check before you re-tag it?
What do you do — right then, on the spot — if you find a pack or mask that doesn't pass during the changeover?
Where do September's completed sheets go when they come out of the trailer?
specialFocus.nonNegotiable: Every trailer flipped on day one: October inspection sheet posted and signed AFTER hands-on checks, new workpacks in, every mask bag opened and re-tagged, SCBA paperwork current. If it didn't get touched, it doesn't get signed.
